overview.title: AI winters and the current AI bubble
overview.main_topic: The two historical AI winters (symbolic AI in the 1960s–70s, expert systems in the 1980s–90s), the authors' assessment of the 2023–2025 AI bubble, and the opening of section 1.12 on AI's long-term promise
overview.central_idea: Inflated short-term expectations have twice led to AI winters when the technology fell short and funding dried up; we are in the optimistic phase of a third cycle, and while a full retreat is unlikely because AI has proven its value, some air must come out of a bubble in which ~$200B of annual investment faces only ~$30B of revenue.
overview.importance: This page gives the historical evidence for the skepticism argued on p.36–37, with concrete dates, quotes and dollar figures, and it states the authors' own forecast for the current cycle. It is the reference point for the book's recurring claim (p.621) that the hype may recede but the impact of deep learning will remain.
learning_objectives: Describe the two historical AI winters: what technology drove each boom (symbolic AI; expert systems), when it happened, and why it collapsed.
Quote or paraphrase Minsky's 1967 and 1970 predictions and explain why the authors cite them.
State the authors' view on the current (third) cycle: unlikely full retreat, a mild winter at most, but a bubble that must deflate.
Give the investment vs. revenue figures the page uses to characterize the 2023–2025 AI bubble and explain what 'judged by what it might become' means.
prerequisites: Symbolic AI and expert systems as defined on p.27 (section 1.3)
The hype discussion of section 1.10 (p.36–37), especially the AGI timelines that this page's Minsky quotes echo

summary:
The page opens by completing p.37's sentence: even with significant advancements, AI will remain a sophisticated tool, not a sentient being — like expecting a better clock to lead to time travel.

**1.11 Summer can turn to winter.** The danger of inflated short-term expectations is that when technology falls short, research investment dries up and progress slows for a long time. This has happened twice. The first cycle began with **symbolic AI in the 1960s**: Marvin Minsky claimed in 1967 that the AI problem would be 'substantially solved' within a generation and in 1970 that 'in from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.' In 2025 that still appears far off — we have no way to predict how long it will take — but experts then (like many people today) thought it was around the corner. When expectations failed, researchers and government funding left the field: the **first AI winter** (named after nuclear winter, shortly after the height of the Cold War). The second cycle came with **expert systems in the 1980s**: early successes triggered corporate in-house AI departments; around 1985 companies spent over $1 billion a year; by the early 1990s the systems proved expensive to maintain, hard to scale and limited in scope, and interest died — the **second AI winter**. We may now be in the **third cycle**, still in the phase of intense optimism.

The author's current view: a full-scale retreat like the 1990s is unlikely; any winter should be very mild, because AI has already demonstrated world-changing value. Still, some air must come out of the **2023–2025 AI bubble**: AI investment, mainly in data centers and GPUs, exceeds **$200 billion per year**, while revenue is closer to **$30 billion**. AI is being judged not on what it has accomplished but on what it is said it might soon do — much of which will 'durably stay out of reach of existing technologies.' Something will have to give; exactly how the bubble deflates is still open.

**1.12 The promise of AI.** Despite unrealistic short-term expectations, the long-term picture is bright: we are only getting started applying deep learning to important problems, from medical diagnoses to digital assistants (continued on p.39).

paragraphs.excerpt: advancements, AI will remain a sophisticated tool, not a sentient being.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Completing the sentence from p.37: even with significant advancements, AI will remain a sophisticated tool rather than a sentient being. Expecting otherwise is like expecting a better clock to lead to time travel — they are different things altogether.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The clock analogy makes a category claim: improving a thing along its own axis (accuracy of a clock; capability of an automation tool) does not turn it into a different kind of thing (a time machine; a sentient mind). Progress in cognitive automation is real but it is progress *within* a category.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the closing line of the AGI argument of section 1.10: the reason not to fear a self-aware takeover is not that progress is slow but that the technology is not of the relevant kind.
connections: p.37: the cartoon vs. living being analogy and the definition of intelligence as adaptability that this sentence concludes.

paragraphs.excerpt: The danger of inflated short-term expectations is that when technology inevitably
paragraphs.what_it_says: Inflated expectations are dangerous because when the technology inevitably falls short, research investment can dry up and slow progress for a long time. This happened twice before, each time as a cycle of intense optimism, disappointment and skepticism, then a dearth of funding. The first began with symbolic AI in the 1960s. Minsky claimed in 1967 that within a generation the AI problem would be substantially solved, and in 1970 that in three to eight years there would be a machine with the general intelligence of an average human. In 2025 that still appears far in the future — there is no way to predict how long it will take — but experts in the 1960s–70s believed it imminent, as many people do today. When the expectations failed, researchers and government funds turned away: the first AI winter, named after nuclear winter because it came shortly after the height of the Cold War.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The paragraph defines the AI hype cycle (optimism → disappointment → funding drought) and gives its first instance. Minsky's two quotes are chosen because they match today's AGI claims almost word for word — a 'quantified' prediction of human-level general intelligence within a few years — and because they were wrong by more than half a century so far. The parenthetical 'as do many people today' ties the history directly to p.37's observation about Bay Area engineers in 2023.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It supplies the historical base rate for confident AGI timelines: the field's most prominent pioneer made one, and it failed badly enough to trigger a funding collapse. The authors' own stance — 'we have no way to predict how long it will take' — is a refusal to give any timeline at all.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): symbolic AI (p.27) tried to hand-write explicit rules; it worked for well-defined logical problems like chess but was intractable for fuzzy perceptual problems, which is part of why the 1960s promises could not be kept.

terminology.meaning: A period of reduced funding and interest in AI following disappointed expectations; the name alludes to nuclear winter.
The paradigm of handcrafting explicit rules and knowledge (p.27); dominant from the 1950s to the late 1980s.
A leading pioneer and proponent of symbolic AI, cited for his 1967 and 1970 predictions.

connections: p.27: symbolic AI defined; it proved intractable for fuzzy problems like image classification.
p.37: OpenAI's 2016 'AGI by 2020' pitch — the modern counterpart of Minsky's 1970 prediction.

paragraphs.excerpt: It wouldn’t be the last one. In the 1980s, a new take on symbolic AI, expert systems
paragraphs.what_it_says: The second winter: in the 1980s expert systems, a new take on symbolic AI, gained traction with large companies. A few early success stories triggered a wave of investment and in-house corporate AI departments; around 1985 companies spent over $1 billion a year. By the early 1990s the systems proved expensive to maintain, difficult to scale and limited in scope, and interest died down — the second AI winter. We may now be in the third cycle of hype and disappointment, still in the optimistic phase.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The second cycle followed the same shape as the first but was driven by corporate rather than government money, and it collapsed on practical engineering grounds (maintenance cost, scalability, narrow scope) rather than on a missed grand prediction. The authors then place the present day on the same curve — explicitly at the *optimism* stage.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The three failure modes of expert systems — expensive to maintain, hard to scale, limited in scope — are a useful checklist for evaluating any AI deployment, and the sentence 'we're still in the phase of intense optimism' is the authors' honest placement of the reader's own moment on the cycle.

terminology.meaning: 1980s symbolic-AI systems encoding domain-expert knowledge as explicit rules; the peak of symbolic AI's popularity (p.27).

connections: p.27: expert systems boom of the 1980s named as symbolic AI's peak.
p.621: the conclusions call the current period 'the third and by far the largest AI summer.'

paragraphs.excerpt: My current view is that we’re unlikely to see a full-scale retreat
paragraphs.what_it_says: The author's view: a full-scale retreat from AI research like the 1990s is unlikely; if a winter comes it should be very mild, because AI has already demonstrated world-changing value. Nevertheless, some air will have to come out of the 2023–2025 AI bubble: annual AI investment, mostly in data centers and GPUs, surpasses $200 billion, while revenue is closer to $30 billion. AI is being judged by executives and investors on what it is said it might soon do — much of which will durably stay out of reach of existing technologies — rather than on what it has accomplished. Something will have to give, but exactly how the bubble deflates is still up in the air.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is a nuanced forecast with three parts: (1) the technology's demonstrated value makes a 1990s-style collapse unlikely; (2) the *financial* side is nonetheless a bubble, quantified by a roughly 7:1 gap between investment and revenue; (3) the bubble is sustained by promised future capabilities, many of which the author believes current technology cannot reach (echoing p.37's automation-vs-intelligence argument). The author is careful to separate the fate of AI research from the fate of the investment cycle.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It tells the reader what kind of 'winter' to prepare for — an investment correction, not an abandonment of the field — and it links the bubble directly to the AGI claims of p.37: the gap is being financed by expectations the authors consider unrealistic.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): the figures are the author's mid-2025 estimates and are stated approximately ('surpasses', 'closer to'); the point is the order-of-magnitude mismatch, not the exact numbers. Compare p.36, which puts generative-AI revenue at 'tens of billions of dollars per year'.

terminology.meaning: The author's term for the period in which AI investment (~$200B/yr, mostly data centers and GPUs) far exceeds AI revenue (~$30B/yr).

connections: p.36: 'As of mid-2025, generative AI was generating tens of billions of dollars in revenue per year' — consistent with the ~$30B figure here.
p.37: 'much of which will durably stay out of reach' restates the claim that current technology is cognitive automation, not intelligence.
p.39: the dot-com comparison — overhyped in 1998–1999, crash, then the internet transformed everything anyway.

paragraphs.excerpt: Although we may have unrealistic short-term expectations for AI, the long-term picture
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 1.12 opens: although short-term expectations may be unrealistic, the long-term picture is bright. We are only getting started applying deep learning to many important problems where it could be transformative, from medical diagnoses to digital assistants.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The pivot from skepticism to optimism. The authors distinguish two time horizons: short-term (hype, bubble, possible mild winter) and long-term (broad transformative deployment). The two examples — medical diagnosis and digital assistants — are chosen from the application list of p.36.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This sets up p.39, where the authors quote their own 2017 predictions and check them against 2025, and the book's summarizing motto: don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.
connections: p.39: the 2017 prediction list and its 2025 scorecard; 'AI is coming.'
p.36: medical imaging assistance and chatbots among the achievements listed in section 1.9.

concepts.name: AI winter
concepts.definition: A period of disappointment, skepticism and scarce funding that follows a phase of intense optimism about AI when the technology falls short of inflated expectations.
concepts.intuition: A boom-and-bust cycle for research funding, named by analogy with nuclear winter.
concepts.technical: Two instances are documented on the page: (1) after the symbolic-AI optimism of the 1960s and Minsky's 1967/1970 predictions, researchers and government funds left the field; (2) after the 1980s expert-systems boom (>$1B/yr corporate spending c. 1985), systems proved expensive to maintain, hard to scale and limited in scope, and interest died by the early 1990s.
concepts.significance: The mechanism — over-promising leads to under-delivery leads to withdrawal of investment — is the practical reason the authors warn against short-term hype: it can slow progress for a long time.
concepts.example: The first AI winter began a few years after Minsky's 1970 claim that a machine with average human general intelligence was three to eight years away.
concepts.misconception: That an AI winter means the ideas were wrong. The authors' view is that the current technology has demonstrated real value, so a third winter, if any, would be mild and would mostly be a correction of the investment bubble.

concepts.name: AI hype cycle
concepts.definition: The recurring sequence of intense optimism, disappointment and skepticism, then a dearth of funding, that AI has gone through twice and may be going through a third time.
concepts.intuition: Summer can turn to winter: each boom carries the seed of the following bust in its unkept promises.
concepts.technical: Cycle 1: symbolic AI, 1960s–early 1970s. Cycle 2: expert systems, 1980s–early 1990s. Cycle 3 (possible): deep learning / generative AI, 2023–2025 and ongoing, currently in the optimism phase.
concepts.significance: Locating the present on the cycle tells practitioners what to expect and lets them tell world-changing developments from overhyped press releases (p.25).
concepts.example: In early 2023 pundits predicted mass unemployment within a year and 10–100× productivity gains; two years later none of it had happened (p.36).
concepts.misconception: That the third cycle must end like the previous two. The authors argue that, unlike earlier summers, deep learning has delivered enormous business and consumer value, so a full-scale retreat is unlikely.

concepts.name: The 2023–2025 AI bubble
concepts.definition: The author's characterization of a period in which AI investment (over $200B/yr, mainly data centers and GPUs) far exceeds AI revenue (around $30B/yr), sustained by expectations of future capabilities.
concepts.intuition: Investors are paying for what AI is said to become, not for what it has done.
concepts.technical: The gap is roughly 7:1. The author expects it must narrow ('something will have to give') but considers a mild winter rather than a 1990s-style retreat most likely, because much of the technology's value is already demonstrated. Much of the promised future capability, the author says, will durably remain out of reach of existing technologies.
concepts.significance: It is the concrete, present-day form of the hype the chapter warns about, and it connects the economics of AI to the technical argument of p.37 about the limits of cognitive automation.
concepts.example: Being judged 'not by what it has accomplished, but by what we are told it might soon become able to do.'
concepts.misconception: That a bubble implies the technology is worthless. The dot-com comparison on p.39 is the authors' model: overhyped, a crash, then genuine long-term transformation.

concepts.name: Expert systems
concepts.definition: 1980s systems, a new take on symbolic AI, that encoded expert knowledge as explicit rules; adopted by large companies that built in-house AI departments.
concepts.intuition: Write down what the expert knows as if-then rules and let the machine apply them.
concepts.technical: Around 1985 corporate spending exceeded $1B per year. By the early 1990s they proved expensive to maintain (rules had to be hand-edited), difficult to scale and limited in scope, and interest collapsed.
concepts.significance: Their failure triggered the second AI winter and, as p.27 explains, motivated the shift from symbolic AI to machine learning, which learns rules from data instead of hand-coding them.
concepts.example: Corporations around the world starting their own in-house AI departments to develop expert systems.
concepts.misconception: That expert systems failed because they never worked. They had initial successes; they failed on the economics of maintenance, scaling and scope.

deeper.title: The three cycles side by side
deeper.body:
Everything in this table is taken from the page (the 'what failed' column for cycle 3 is the author's prediction, not an outcome):

| Cycle | Technology | Boom | Signature promise | What failed | Bust |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Symbolic AI | 1960s | Minsky 1967: solved 'within a generation'; 1970: human-level general intelligence in 3–8 years | Expectations did not materialize | First AI winter (early–mid 1970s; researchers and government funds withdraw) |
| 2 | Expert systems (symbolic AI) | 1980s; >$1B/yr by ~1985 | In-house corporate AI departments | Expensive to maintain, hard to scale, limited in scope | Second AI winter (early 1990s) |
| 3 (possible) | Deep learning / generative AI | 2023–2025; >$200B/yr investment vs ~$30B revenue | Mass unemployment, 10–100× productivity (p.36), near-term AGI (p.37) | Much of the promised capability will 'durably stay out of reach' | Author expects a mild correction, not a full retreat |

deeper.title: Reading the $200B vs $30B gap
deeper.body:
The page gives annual AI investment as 'surpassing $200 billion' and revenue as 'closer to $30 billion'. Taking the figures at face value:

- Ratio: $200\text{B} / $30\text{B} \approx 6.7$, i.e. roughly seven dollars invested for every dollar of revenue.
- Even if revenue grew at the remarkable pace noted on p.36 (an industry that did not exist three years earlier is already making tens of billions), it would need to grow several-fold before it matched a single year's investment — and investment is mostly in depreciating assets (GPUs, data centers).

This is why the author concludes 'something will have to give': either revenue catches up, or investment falls, or both. The author does not predict which. (This arithmetic is mine; the book only states the two figures.)

deeper.title: Why the author expects the third winter to be mild
deeper.body:
The page's argument can be read as a contrast with the earlier cycles (this reading is an inference):

- In cycles 1 and 2 the technology under-delivered on its *core* promise (general intelligence; maintainable, scalable rule systems), so when the promise failed there was little demonstrated value to fall back on.
- In cycle 3 the inflated promises (AGI, 100× productivity) sit on top of a technology that has *already* produced world-changing value — the list on p.35–36 and the tens of billions in revenue on p.36.

So the author separates two things that collapsed together in the past: belief in the grand promise (which can deflate) and the practical value of the technology (which stays). The conclusions chapter (p.621) makes the same point: 'The hype may (and likely will) recede, but the sustained economic and technological impact of deep learning will remain.'

misconceptions.claim: AI winters are a thing of the distant past; modern AI is immune to them.
misconceptions.correction: The page says we may be in the third cycle and are still in the optimism phase. The authors' claim is only that a *full-scale* retreat is unlikely and that any winter should be mild — not that one is impossible.

misconceptions.claim: The expert-systems boom collapsed because the systems never worked.
misconceptions.correction: They had initial success stories that triggered the investment wave; they collapsed because they were expensive to maintain, difficult to scale and limited in scope.

misconceptions.claim: The $200B vs $30B gap means the author thinks AI is overvalued and will fail.
misconceptions.correction: The author says AI 'has already demonstrated its world-changing value' and that the long-term picture is bright (section 1.12). The gap is evidence of a financial bubble that must deflate, not of a failed technology.

misconceptions.claim: The authors give a timeline for human-level AI.
misconceptions.correction: They explicitly refuse: in 2025 it 'still appears to be far in the future — in that we have no way to predict how long it will take.'

earlier.note: Chapter opener: the goal of telling 'world-changing developments from overhyped press releases.'
Symbolic AI and the expert-systems boom of the 1980s, and why machine learning replaced them.
Opening of section 1.10: early-2023 predictions of mass unemployment and 10–100× productivity that did not come to pass; generative-AI revenue in the tens of billions.
The AGI timelines (2013, 2016, 2023) that parallel Minsky's 1967/1970 predictions; 'much of which will durably stay out of reach' echoes the cognitive-automation argument.

later.note: Section 1.12 continues: the 2017 predictions checked against 2025, the dot-com analogy, and 'Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.'
Chapter 19's history of AI from 1960s automatons (ELIZA, SHRDLU) through machine learning to deep learning.
The 2024 shift away from 'scale is all you need' — an example of promised capabilities requiring new ideas rather than more of the same.
Conclusions: deep learning brought 'the third and by far the largest AI summer'; the hype may recede but the impact will remain, like the internet.

prerequisites.note: Definition of symbolic AI, the paradigm behind both earlier winters.

takeaways: Improving AI makes a better tool, not a sentient being — like a better clock not leading to time travel.
Inflated expectations are dangerous because disappointment dries up research funding and can slow progress for a long time.
First AI winter: symbolic AI's 1960s optimism (Minsky 1967: solved 'within a generation'; 1970: human-level general intelligence in 3–8 years) collapsed in the 1970s.
Second AI winter: 1980s expert systems (>$1B/yr corporate spending by ~1985) proved expensive to maintain, hard to scale and limited in scope; interest died by the early 1990s.
We may be in a third cycle and are still in the phase of intense optimism; the author expects at most a mild winter because AI has already shown world-changing value.
The 2023–2025 AI bubble: >$200B/yr investment (data centers, GPUs) against ~$30B/yr revenue; AI is judged on promised future abilities, many of which will stay out of reach of existing technology.
Short-term expectations may be unrealistic, but the long-term picture is bright — from medical diagnoses to digital assistants, we are only getting started.

questions.question: What caused the end of the expert-systems boom in the early 1990s, according to the page?
options: The systems proved expensive to maintain, difficult to scale, and limited in scope.
Government funding was cut after the Cold War ended.
Deep learning made expert systems obsolete overnight.
Marvin Minsky publicly retracted his predictions.
questions.answer: The systems proved expensive to maintain, difficult to scale, and limited in scope.
questions.explanation: The page lists exactly these three problems. The Cold War reference belongs to the *name* of the first winter, not the cause of the second; deep learning's rise came two decades later; and Minsky's predictions concern the first cycle, not the second.

questions.question: What did Marvin Minsky predict in 1970, and why do the authors quote it?
questions.answer: That 'in from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.' The authors quote it because it is a precisely quantified AGI timeline that failed completely, illustrating how inflated expectations preceded the first AI winter and how similar claims are made today.
questions.explanation: The quote is paired with his 1967 claim ('within a generation') and followed by the remark that in 2025 the achievement still appears far off, with the parenthetical 'as do many people today' linking it to current AGI claims (p.37).

questions.question: Which statement best matches the author's view of the current cycle?
options: A third AI winter as severe as the 1990s is almost certain.
A full-scale retreat is unlikely and any winter should be mild, but the 2023–2025 investment bubble must deflate.
There is no bubble because revenue already matches investment.
AI research will stop entirely once investors lose interest.
questions.answer: A full-scale retreat is unlikely and any winter should be mild, but the 2023–2025 investment bubble must deflate.
questions.explanation: The page: 'we're unlikely to see a full-scale retreat… If there is a winter, it should be very mild… However, it seems inevitable that some air will need to be let out of the 2023–2025 AI bubble.' Revenue (~$30B) is far below investment (>$200B), so the third option is false; the first and fourth overstate the pessimism.

questions.question: Give the approximate annual AI investment and revenue figures the page cites, and state what the author says AI is currently being judged on.
questions.answer: Investment surpasses $200 billion per year (mainly data centers and GPUs); revenue is closer to $30 billion. AI is being judged by executives and investors not on what it has accomplished but on what it is said it might soon become able to do.
questions.explanation: These are the page's own figures and wording; the author adds that much of the promised capability 'will durably stay out of reach of existing technologies,' so 'something will have to give.'

questions.question: Why is the first AI winter called a 'winter', and what general mechanism does the page say produces AI winters?
questions.answer: The name alludes to nuclear winter, since the period came shortly after the height of the Cold War. The mechanism: inflated short-term expectations lead to disappointment when the technology falls short, and then research investment dries up, slowing progress for a long time.
questions.explanation: The page gives both the etymology (in parentheses) and the causal description in its opening sentence: 'when technology inevitably falls short, research investment could dry up, slowing progress for a long time.'

questions.question: The page says 'It's like expecting a better clock to lead to time travel.' What claim about AI is this analogy making?
questions.answer: That improving AI along its current axis (more capable automation) does not change what kind of thing it is: it remains a sophisticated tool, not a sentient being, just as a more accurate clock is still not a time machine.
questions.explanation: This completes the argument of p.37 that today's AI is cognitive automation rather than cognitive autonomy; progress within a category does not produce a different category.

questions.question: Where would you place the present moment on the optimism–disappointment–funding-drought cycle, and which of the page's signals (dollar figures, what AI is being judged on) support your placement?
questions.answer: Open-ended. The authors place it in the phase of intense optimism; a good answer cites the investment/revenue gap and the judgement-by-future-promise as signs that the correction has not yet happened.
questions.explanation: The exercise is to apply the page's historical pattern to the present rather than to memorize it.
